'''John Lane Bell''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|FRSC}} (born March 25, 1945) is a Canadian philosopher, mathematician, and logician specializing in [[mathematical logic]] and the foundations of [[mathematics]]. He served as Professor of Philosophy at the [[University of Western Ontario]] from 1989 until his retirement in 2019, and previously held positions at the [[London School of Economics]] from 1968 to 1989<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Bell |first=John |date=November 2022 |title=Professor John L. Bell |url=https://publish.uwo.ca/~jbell/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008194541/https://publish.uwo.ca/~jbell/ |archive-date=October 8, 2025 |access-date=December 13, 2025}}</ref>. Elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada]] in 2009, Bell's research encompasses [[constructive mathematics]], [[intuitionistic logic]], [[set theory]], [[topos theory]], and the [[axiom of choice]], among other topics.<ref name=":0" />

Bell has authored influential books including ''Intuitionistic Set Theory'' (2014), which explores set-theoretic foundations intuitionistic principles, and ''Oppositions and Paradoxes'' (2016), addressing logical and philosophical [[Paradox|paradoxes]]. His work bridges technical developments in logic with philosophical inquiries into continuity, [[Infinitesimal|infinitesimals]], and the nature of [[Mathematical structure|mathematical structures]], contributing to the ongoing debates in the [[philosophy of mathematics]].<ref name=":0" />

==Biography==
John Bell was awarded a scholarship to [[Oxford University]] at the age of 15, and graduated with a D.Phil. in Mathematics: his dissertation supervisor was [[John Crossley (mathematician)|John Crossley]]. During 1968–89 he was Lecturer in Mathematics and Reader in Mathematical Logic at the [[London School of Economics]].<ref name="bellbio1">{{cite web|url=https://publish.uwo.ca/~jbell/|title=Professor John L. Bell|publisher=University of Western Ontario|access-date=25 March 2010}}</ref>

Bell's students include [[Graham Priest]] (Ph.D. Mathematics LSE, 1972), [[Michael Hallett]] (Ph.D. Philosophy LSE, 1979), [[David DeVidi]] (Ph.D. Philosophy UWO, 1994), [[Elaine Landry]] (Ph.D. Philosophy UWO, 1997) and [[Richard A. Feist]] (Ph.D. Philosophy UWO, 1999).
